title: Photo-sharing app
summary: Post photos, follow people, scroll a feed: presigned uploads into a resizing pipeline, a CDN serving 460 Gbps of images, a hybrid fan-out feed, and like counters that survive a 100M-follower account.
interviewerPrompt: Design a photo-sharing app. People post photos with captions, follow each other, and scroll a home feed of posts from accounts they follow, where they can like and comment. Where would you start?

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many users, and how active are they?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 500M daily active users on phones, out of roughly 1B accounts. Assume the busiest hour is about twice the daily average.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many photos are posted, and how big are they?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 100M new photos a day, averaging 2 MB as uploaded. One photo per post is a fine simplification.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How much do people scroll?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 50 feed images per user per day, roughly 5 feed pages of 10 posts each.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How skewed is the follow graph?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The average account follows about 150 others, but some accounts have 100M followers.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How fast must the feed load?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Under 500 ms at p99 on mobile networks, measured on the device. Images can stream in after the feed's text and layout.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does 'never lose a photo' mean exactly?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Once the app tells the user their post is shared, the photo must survive any single machine, disk or zone failure.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How quickly must a new post appear in followers' feeds?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Within seconds for most followers. A minute is acceptable for accounts with huge followings.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many likes and comments?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 5 per user per day combined, mostly likes. Counts shown on a post may lag by a few seconds but must not drift permanently.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the feed chronological or ranked?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Ranked, but ranking itself is out of scope: assume a ranking service orders a few hundred candidates you give it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are videos, stories, direct messages or search in scope?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Photos, follows, the home feed, likes and comments only.

deepDiveQuestions: How does a photo get from the phone to followers' screens: presigned upload, resizing into variants, and never losing an acknowledged photo?
How do you store and serve billions of images cheaply: variants, formats, CDN cache keys and storage tiers?
How do you build the home feed when the average account has 150 followers but some have 100M?
How do you count likes and comments at 58,000 writes per second so counts are fast to read and never drift?
What happens in the minutes after an account with 100M followers posts, and how do you keep hot keys from melting the cache and database?

runChallenge.title: Cold cache at the evening peak
runChallenge.description: At the 2× peak (about 579,000 image fetches, 58,000 feed loads and 58,000 likes or comments per second), the Redis cluster is flushed 10 s in. Ten seconds later, with the cache still mostly cold, feed loads must stay under 250 ms at p99 server-side with almost no errors, and no single component may be able to take the feed down.

commonMistakes: Uploading photo bytes through the API servers instead of straight to object storage with a presigned URL, so 37 Gbps of ingress and slow mobile uploads tie up request threads.
Serving the 2 MB original to every phone instead of resized variants, multiplying CDN egress and slowing the feed on mobile networks.
Fanning out every post to every follower's timeline, so one post from a 100M-follower account means 100M timeline writes.
Storing a like count as a single row incremented on every like, which becomes a hot row the moment a celebrity posts.
Keeping likes only as a counter, with no per-user like record, so double taps double count and 'did I like this?' cannot be answered.
Acknowledging a post before the photo is durably stored, or deleting the phone's local copy before the server confirms, which loses photos on a crash.
Sizing the database for the cache's steady-state miss rate only, so a cold cache sends the full feed load to a store that cannot take it.
Paginating the feed with offsets, which shows duplicates and skips posts as new posts arrive at the top.
